The choice of diffusion
$$
dY_t^\varepsilon
 =\frac12\beta(t)(\widetilde u+u)(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)\,dt+dB_t,
\qquad Y_0^\varepsilon=0,
$$
cancels the first-order spatial term when Itô's formula is applied to
$D(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)$. Its drift has absolute value at most $\beta(t)$,
which is integrable. On $[0,T]$ the resulting identity is
$$
D(0,0)=\mathbb E D(T,Y_T^\varepsilon)
 +\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_0^T
       \eta(t)\mathbb E[u(t,Y_t^\varepsilon)^2]\,dt.
$$

lean.note: Only the sampled slopes are stated here. Convexity gives the full right derivative in the paper.

statements.markdown:
The manuscript's first variation and its formal counterpart differ in one
useful respect. The formal result initially gives a derivative
along chord lengths $1/(n+1)$. For this particular control functional,
that sampled limit determines the ordinary feasible right derivative.
With a control fixed, the terminal absolute value is convex in the
coefficient while the penalty is linear. The supremum over the same
control class, and then subtraction of the linear Parisi penalty,
preserve convexity.

The secant slopes therefore vary monotonically as the chord shortens, and
each intervening chord lies between two successive
sampled chords and has the same limiting slope. If $\eta$ is an
integrable feasible direction, choose $\varepsilon_0>0$ so that
$\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ is admissible and rescale the chord. This
bridge is an ordinary deduction from the definitions and the sampled
limit, and no separately named formal theorem states it.
statements.section: 12.1 The support statement and the derivative bridge

statements.markdown:
When $\gamma$ is replaced by $\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$ and
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the functional changes at the rate
$$
D_+\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta]
=\tfrac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt,                 \tag{1}
$$
for every integrable direction $\eta$ for which
$\gamma+\varepsilon\eta\in\mathcal U$ for all sufficiently small
$\varepsilon\geq0$ (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1][FS], and
[Chen, Handschy and Lerman (2018), Propositions 3–4][CHL] for the
earlier zero-temperature form).

statements.markdown:
**[Question 1](#question-1).** Adding mass at $1/2$ gives cumulative heights
$0,2,2+\varepsilon,3+\varepsilon$, in their successive intervals;
removing it at $1/4$ gives heights $0,2-\varepsilon,3-\varepsilon$.
Both functions remain nonnegative and nondecreasing.

Removing mass at
$1/2$ instead lowers the height from $2$ to $2-\varepsilon$ there,
creating a downward jump, so it is forbidden even though all values
remain nonnegative.
statements.note: Not in the Lean: this example. removeCDF needs ν≤μ, which fails with no mass at 1/2; the Lean proves nothing about this candidate.

statements.markdown:
As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the coefficients converge in $L^1$ and have
uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms. On each fixed strip, their gradients converge
uniformly and have common spatial Lipschitz bounds. Coupling with the same
Brownian motion and applying Gronwall's inequality therefore gives
$Y^\varepsilon\to X$ uniformly on that strip.
